To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
medical abortions are provided in pharmacies and drug shops throughout low‐ and middle ‐ income countries, but there is limited evidence on interventions that improve the quality of provision.
there is limited evidence on pharmacy and drug shop delivery of medical abortion (mifepristone and misoprostol), and that training of pharmacy workers is effective in improving knowledge.

Medical abortion provision in pharmacies and drug sellers in low‐ and mid‐income countries is widespread despite legal restrictions, however, most studies have found pharmacy workers and drug shop providers have poor knowledge about effective regimens.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: How do pharmacies and drug sellers in low‐and‐middle‐income countries (LMIICs) provide medical abortion services?
the provision of medical abortion in low‐and mid‐income countries.
the role of pharmacies and drug sellers in providing safe, effective, and accessible medical abortion (MA).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Medical abortion provision by pharmacies and drug shops in LMICs is widespread, despite restrictive laws in many countries.

there is a lack of evidence of the quality of medical abortion provision through pharmacies and other outlets in low- and middle-income countries, and that the evidence of interventions to improve quality is also limited.
there is limited and low‐quality evidence that training of pharmacists and drug shop workers can increase the provision of medical abortion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the quality of MA provision in pharmacies and drug sellers in LMICs is generally poor, and that there is a need to develop and evaluate effective training interventions to improve quality.
medical abortion is an effective method of early pregnancy termination that can be safely provided in pharmacies and drug sellers.
there is a lack of evidence on the level and quality, and interventions to improve quality, of pharmacy and drug seller provision of medical abortion.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the evidence base on pharmacy and drug shop medical abortion provision and quality of care in low‐ and mid‐income countries is limited, with few studies on the quality of care and even fewer intervention studies.
there is a gap in knowledge of the quality of MA provision by pharmacies and drug sellers in low‐ and mid‐income countries.
there is a need to improve pharmacy and other private sector drug shop provision of MVA in low‐ and lower middle‐income countries, where the majority of women obtain abortion services.
